Furthermore, protracted climate hazards can also erode individuals’ mental health. A literature review concluded that rising temperatures and more frequent extreme weather events contribute to psychological distress that heightens the risk for interpersonal conflict (Evans, 2019). The mere awareness of climate change and its potential consequences on human livelihoods and survival can also be associated with chronic anxiety (or “ecoanxiety”), distress, hopelessness, and reduced well-being, which is visible particularly in children and adolescents and can relate to externalizing and internalizing behavior pro­ blems and compromise children’s cognitive, social, and emotional development (Martin et al., 2022; Palinkas & Wong, 2020). Finally, a review of 26 studies also found that climate change is impacting the mental health of Indigenous communities, exacerbating depression, sadness, suicidal ideation, and loss of communities’ culture and identity due to changes in the physical environment, restricted mobility, and disrupted livelihoods (Lebel et al., 2022).

Development Experiencing climate hazards early in life can be particularly consequential because chil­ dren’s developing biological systems are more vulnerable to environmental threats such as heat, pollutants, lack of clean water and adequate nutrition, and zoonotic and other diseases (Cuartas et al., 2024; Sanson et al., 2022; Vergunst & Berry, 2024). For example, young children’s small bodies heat up more quickly and are less capable of regulating body temperature via sweating relative to adults (Early Childhood Scientific Council on Equity and the Environment, 2023). Similarly, the developing brain detects excessive heat, pollu­ tants, extreme weather, and other climate hazards as threats, activating the stress response system and triggering physiological (e.g., cortisol release) and psychological (e.g., fear) consequences. While these responses can be adaptive and help ensure physical safety and survival, repeated activation of the stress response system or chronic stress can undermine brain and foundational skill development (Early Childhood Scientific Council on Equity and the Environment, 2023).

While there is substantially less evidence about the potential impacts of climate change on child developmental outcomes relative to health outcomes, existing studies indicate climate change may interfere with children’s healthy development. A literature review of more than 100 studies found evidence that exposure to air pollution can undermine the development of cognitive, motor, social, and emotional skills that predict lifelong health, learning, and behavior (Cuartas et al., 2024). The same review showed that extreme temperatures and floods are also associated with negative cognitive, social, and emotional outcomes, and exposure to vector-borne diseases, such as the Zika virus, can alter the healthy development of foundational cognitive skills.

Outcomes for the family system

Marriage and reproductive behavior Growing evidence shows a complex interplay between climate change and reproductive behavior, with nuanced and context-specific dynamics. Evidence from more than 114,000 women who participated in Demographic and Health Surveys from 17 African countries

showed that drought exposure predicted fertility preferences in most countries, with women expressing desires to hasten or delay having another child, but these results were not consistent across all countries (Somefun et al., 2024). This study found little evidence for associations between drought and access to contraceptive methods (with statistically sig­ nificant associations only in three countries).

There is also evidence from large scale surveys in Bangladesh, India, Malawi, Nepal, and Pakistan that exposure to growing-season drought and floods during adolescence relates to faster transitions into first unions and early marriage and cohabitation, as well as teenage pregnancy (Andriano & Behrman, 2020; Dietrich et al., 2022). Findings from a scoping review of 24 studies from South and South-East Asia indicate that climate hazards like droughts, floods, and heat waves can exacerbate drivers of child marriage, such as forced displacement, loss of assets, educational disruption, and heightened contextual risk that facilitates sexual violence or the fear of sexual violence (Pope et al., 2023). The impacts of these socioeconomic pressures and environmental stressors that prompt families to resort to early marriage may be even stronger in settings with social norms that legitimize early marriages (Asadullah et al., 2021). In turn, early marriages compromise young parents’ developmental trajectories and can increase the risk for negative health and developmental outcomes for children (Efevbera et al., 2017).

Physical closeness and separation About 80% of forcibly displaced people in 2022 were displaced due to climate hazards, and the United Nations estimates that about 700 million people may be displaced due to drought alone (UNHCR, 2024). Existing evidence supports the idea that climate changerelated migration may affect physical closeness and separation in the family system. For instance, a study with about 79,000 participants in rural India found associations between experience of drought and the probability of a household having at least one temporary migrant member, with stronger associations for socioeconomically marginalized families compared to their better-off peers (Sarkar et al., 2022). In contrast, a U.S. study used a quasi-experimental approach and found increased family physical closeness after experi­ encing a tornado compared to pre-tornado levels (Wang et al., 2022). This inconsistency may be due to the nature of exposure (droughts are protracted whereas tornadoes are shorter in duration), but more research is needed.

Relationships and conflict Considering that climate change may induce stress and health challenges in individual family members, it is likely that it could also lead to further stress in the family system as a whole, affecting relationships and increasing conflict. Two longitudinal studies from the U.S. found contradictory evidence in this regard, with one (Hammett et al., 2022) showing increased risk for marital conflict after a hurricane, suggesting a detrimental effect on spouses’ relationships, whereas the second found temporary increases in marital satisfaction after hurricane exposure (Williamson et al., 2021). Another study found that country-level climate change-related hazards (e.g., increases in greenhouse gas emissions and extreme temperatures) are related to rising divorce rates (Huang & Ma, 2024). While these findings are mixed and largely correlational, an ethnographic study in Burkina Faso found that a group of 40 women perceived that excessive heat interfered with their relationships with their partners, the care they provided to their children, and increased feelings of family

Additional evidence indicates that, although climate hazards pressure the family system, family relationships can also strengthen in the context of climate change. A review of 20 studies (Ayalon et al., 2022) indicates that younger family members tend to believe that older generations neither fully understand nor care about climate change and exclude young people from discussions about it. The same review found that intergenerational relationships can be strengthened when older generations engage in the climate change movement and young people can share their experiences and perspectives on climate change. Another study of 19 families in Canada (Pujadas Botey & Kulig, 2014) showed significant changes in family routines and interactions after experiencing climate disasters, with increases in closeness and use of collective coping mechanisms critical to promoting resilience.

Parenting and child maltreatment Some nascent evidence indicates that climate change may affect some parenting behaviors. For example, Brando and Santos (2014) studied a longitudinal sample of more than 2,000 children and their parents before and after a season of atypical heavy rains in Colombia. They not only found that exposure to heavy rains was related to increases in child socialemotional problems and reduced cognitive performance, but also that exposed parents talked less to their children, on average. The authors found no associations between exposure to heavy rains and other parenting behaviors, such as engagement in play and other learning activities.

Some authors have also argued that the strain caused by climate change can exacerbate the risk of child maltreatment (Cuartas et al., 2023). Consistent with this idea, a study of 118 children living in an area affected by a major hurricane in the U.S. found post-hurricane increases in parental hostility, which subsequently predicted increases in children’s aggres­ sive behavior (Terranova et al., 2015). Similarly, a retrospective study of more than 27,000 adults in the United States found that experiencing climate hazards (e.g., fires, hurricanes) early in life was associated with increased reports of child abuse (Maclean et al., 2016). Yet, the same study also found somewhat contradictory evidence of associations between climate hazards exposure and reports of increased emotional support in childhood. This finding may reflect the complex challenges parents face when coping with the stress of climate hazards while simultaneously striving to provide support to their children.

Intimate partner violence To date, there is some evidence that intimate partner violence may increase in the context of climate change, indicating the gendered nature of climate change impacts on families, but these associations require further examination and might be highly context-specific. Four independent studies using household survey data provided inconclusive evidence for links between climate hazards and intimate partner violence. The first study (Epstein et al., 2020) examined a sample of about 80,000 15–49-year-old women in Sub-Saharan Africa and found that those who experienced severe drought were more likely to report a controlling partner and experiences of physical and sexual abuse relative to women who did not experience the drought. The second study of 149,000 women from 17 countries (Cools et al., 2020) found little evidence that atypical rainfall patterns were related to intimate

Finally, one study with data from Mozambique, Uganda, and Zimbabwe showed increases of 25% to 91% in women’s reports of intimate partner violence in regions affected by extreme weather events relative to areas not affected (Munala et al., 2023).

The review showed that in some cases, there were increases in gender-based violence during or after extreme weather events, probably due to the consequences of disasters on critical drivers of violence (e.g., economic insecurity, psychological distress, and heightened gender inequality). Yet, the review also included some studies that reported no significant increases in gender-based violence after extreme weather events and even reductions in sexual violence in some cases. Considering extensive evidence linking intimate partner violence and adverse child development outcomes (Jeong et al., 2020), increased risk for intimate partner violence may be one mechanism linking climate change and negative human development across the life course.

Limitations reported in prior studies

The reviews and primary studies included here identified significant limitations in prior research. First, several studies found significant variability in the way climate change-related hazards are conceptualized and measured, often overlooking some climate hazards (e.g., protracted hazards) and exposure in multiple settings (e.g., Ma et al., 2022; van Daalen et al., 2022). Several studies also commented on the use of poor measurement approaches, such as low-resolution measurement of climate hazards and self-reported outcomes or exposure measures (e.g., Evans, 2019; Hammett et al., 2022). Inadequate conceptual work has led to many studies being data-driven instead of theory-driven, which, along with weaknesses in measurement, limits their validity and makes it difficult to draw meaningful comparisons between studies (Lu, 2020).

Second, there is inadequate examination of developmental issues and variation in observed effects in research to date. For instance, most research has focused on the impacts of single climate hazards, but these hazards may operate in additive and interactive ways (Shah et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2016). There is emerging evidence on whether experiencing multiple climate hazards may increase risks, and whether and how household character­ istics (e.g., wealth) and behaviors (e.g., mitigation and adaptation behaviors) may moderate observed associations (Kuehn & McCormick, 2017; Thompson et al., 2023). There is also less work on the potential consequences of climate hazards for children and adolescents relative to adults, despite the fact that younger people may be at heightened risk of detrimental outcomes due to their immaturity and developmental plasticity (Blanc et al., 2023; Cuartas et al., 2024; Lebel et al., 2022).

Finally, additional methodological shortcomings limit the internal (i.e., causal conclu­ sions) and external validity (i.e., generalizability) of previous findings. Existing reviews identified a high risk of publication bias and an overreliance on conventional covariate

## Discussion

Climate change-related hazards are now more salient than ever, and they will continue to affect families worldwide (e.g., Rees, 2021; Trask, 2020). Still, there has been scarce research on the links between climate change, family outcomes, and human development more broadly. Studying the potential impacts of climate change on families, and not only individual outcomes, is important because it is within the family system that these effects can be mitigated or amplified and experienced collectively, impacting dynamics, relation­ ships, and the well-being of all members with downstream consequences on individual outcomes, creating potential (virtuous or vicious) cycles.

This review revealed extensive evidence for links between climate change and outcomes for individual family members. Consistent evidence across many different studies indicates that climate change-related hazards, such as excessive heat, pollution, and extreme weather events, can compromise individuals’ physical and mental health. These results are consis­ tent with our bioecological and dynamic systems model (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2007; Thelen & Smith, 1998), which shows the role of contextual hazards at both proximal and distal levels of the developmental ecology. We also found evidence, though less extensive, of links between climate change and a range of child development outcomes. These findings resonate with developmental theory and research showing that climate hazards may be particularly consequential early in life when biological systems and cognitive and emotional skills are still in formation and develop rapidly in response to experiences and environments (Vergunst & Berry, 2024).

We also found emerging, but scarcer, evidence that climate change can affect families’ composition, closeness, and relationships, in most cases increasing the risk for detrimental outcomes such as gender-based violence. These results align with multiple conceptual perspectives and empirical evidence on how contextual hazards can increase family stress and reduce families’ resources and capabilities to deal with internal and external threats, ultimately affecting relationships and exacerbating the risk for detrimental outcomes, such as violent behavior, which threaten individual family members’ health and development (Bornstein, 2015). At the same time, some evidence suggests that exposure to climate hazards can increase family closeness and strengthen relationships, exemplifying the prin­ ciple of resilience in human development (Masten, 2016).

Implications for policy and practice

The present study illustrates that climate change already threatens families around the world. However, the extent to which these consequences escalate depends on current decision-making (IPCC, 2023). Swift action is therefore needed to protect, strengthen,

Policies and interventions can support families and promote healthy development by: (1) preventing families from experiencing the negative consequences of climate change by mitigating risks before they occur; (2) preparing families to face the negative consequences that are already underway; (3) supporting families as they face climate hazards; and (4) engaging families in responding to climate change and developing climate policy. There are roles for researchers and practitioners in psychology and related disciplines in achieving these goals.

By mitigating risks before they occur, policies that slow, and ideally reverse, the devel­ opment of human-induced climate change have the greatest potential to prevent families from being negatively affected by climate hazards. The wellbeing of current and future families ultimately relies on the rapid reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and the drawing down of excess greenhouse gases already in the atmosphere. Indeed, such emis­ sions are the root cause of the vast number of climate hazards that can directly or indirectly harm families. Developmental scientists thus have an important role in communicating relevant scientific evidence and encouraging urgent policy changes to reduce emissions rapidly, so as to protect family wellbeing and prevent harm.

With climate change already underway, programs and policies are needed to help families prepare for the impacts of climate change. For example, community-level disaster risk assessments (e.g., risk of wildfires, landslides), disaster prevention planning (e.g., firebreaks, relocating schools and hospitals), and disaster preparedness (e.g., developing an evacuation plan) can help families feel more confident, in control, and better able to make effective emergency plans when a disaster is imminent (Australian Psychological Society, 2020a). Especially in high-income countries, instructions for families responding to natural disasters may already exist (e.g., CDC, 2024). However, fewer resources are available to help families understand – and communicate with youth about – the more protracted threats of climate change (e.g., desertification, which may require families to relocate and/or find an alternative source of financial security). Creating and widely disseminating such resources can help families preempt the threats of climate change to secure their own wellbeing. Families can also benefit from instruction in how to recognize climate dis/misinformation, speak with youth about climate change, and help young people develop effective coping strategies to deal with climate distress (e.g., Ojala, 2023). Developmental scientists can also help preparation efforts by advocating for adaptation policies and plans, for instance, to ensure that families’ homes, schools, health facilities, and other critical infrastructure are strong enough to withstand increasingly extreme weather events (e.g., Climate Resiliency Design Guidelines by the NYC Mayor’s Office of Climate and Environmental Justice). As climate impacts can exacerbate existing inequalities, targeted policies and programs are needed to support the most vulnerable communities and families.

Policies and interventions also need to be in place to support families when they are negatively affected by both acute and chronic climate hazards. Supports need to cover a wide range of issues, including physical health, mental health, education, parenting, housing, and economic wellbeing. As one example, psychological first aid is often essential to supporting families’ recovery post-disaster. Psychological first aid uses basic principles of psychosocial support to promote natural recovery by helping people feel safe, connected to others, calm, and hopeful, and ensuring access to physical, emotional, and social support (Australian Psychological Society, 2020b). In addition to health, economic wellbeing can be compromised in climate disasters, and cash transfer programs can alleviate economic

Moreover, gender-transformative parenting programs can be a promising strategy to promote positive family relationships and simultaneously prevent violence against women and violence against children (Jeong et al., 2021; UNICEF Innocenti - Global Office of Research and Foresight, Prevention Collaborative, & Equimundo, 2023).

Programs and policies can also engage families in responding proactively to climate change by encouraging them to adopt sustainable lifestyles and involving them in the development of interventions and policies. Families serve as an elementary unit of society, so policies that enable families to adopt more sustainable practices (e.g., subsidies for families to install heat pumps; European Heat Pump Association, 2023) can help spur the sustainable transitions needed throughout society. However, families need access to infor­ mation and resources to be able to spearhead such change. For example, research in Egypt among urban and rural communities found that many families were responding proactively to climate change, such as by insulating their homes. Still, 50% of those who had not yet taken action were unable to do so because they lacked information (Froehlich & Al-Saidi, 2018). To engage youth, providing environmental education as part of national curricula can improve environmental outcomes and set the stage for a more sustainable future. Developmental science can inform the creation of such curricula and interventions by making them more likely to support behavior change among different age groups (Thomaes et al., 2023). Including individuals and families, especially from traditionally underrepre­ sented and disadvantaged communities, in the process of developing policies and interven­ tions can also enhance their uptake, relevance, and capacity to contribute to more fair and equitable societies. For example, there are some initiatives to make Indigenous communities partners in clean energy projects (e.g., the 2023 Aboriginal Clean Energy Partnership in Australia, a 75% indigenous-owned green hydrogen venture). By engaging families in developing and adopting climate solutions, policymakers can better respond to their needs and expand upon their strengths.

These adaptation strategies enhance existing disaster response frameworks by addressing the unique contexts, capacities, and resources of LMICs. High-income countries (HICs) often benefit from advanced infrastructure, insurance schemes, and centralized coordina­ tion, easing the recovery burden. In contrast, while LMIC communities demonstrate resilience, recurring climate-related challenges and resource constraints disproportionately strain families and local systems. To break this cycle of vulnerability, preemptive strategies are crucial. By implementing sustainable, context-specific solutions, these adaptations strengthen long-term resilience and mitigate recurring risks. Further efforts are needed to tailor existing frameworks to diverse settings, fostering more inclusive and sustainable disaster preparedness and response systems globally.

Our review highlighted that climate hazards not only affect individuals but also have profound impacts on social connections, family dynamics, and household functioning. Research and policies that focus solely on individuals risk overlooking these broader familylevel influences. Families play a pivotal role in fostering intergenerational dialogs that connect past, present, and future experiences (Zurba et al., 2020). By actively engaging in such efforts, they can help break cycles of vulnerability, ease recovery burdens, and promote equity within and beyond their communities. Integrating families into multi-stakeholder discussions for climate policy and intervention design offers a more effective alternative to

Limitations and future directions for research

The present study has limitations that, along with those identified in the reviewed studies (as summarized in the Results section), can inform future research. First, although we adopted a conceptual framework based on bioecological and dynamic systems perspectives, there is still a need for more conceptual work, clarification, and standardization of definitions (e.g., what do we mean when we say climate change and families?), and conceptualizing how different features of climate hazards (e.g., severity, chronicity, pervasiveness) may lead to specific family outcomes, considering additive and interactive effects. Future research could also employ strong theoretical insights to conduct extensive measurement work, including leveraging higher resolution data about climate hazards and measurement of specific features of climate change-related hazards to study questions such as: What are the impacts of climate change on family relationships? Does climate change exacerbate violence against women and children? Are there heterogeneous gender-based effects of climate change on child and adult health and development? and how do the effects of climate change on family and individual outcomes vary across different countries and socioeconomic groups?

Second, this study used a rapid review approach, so it is not an exhaustive exploration of the literature and does not provide a quantitative synthesis of the associations between exposure to climate change-related hazards and family outcomes. Furthermore, given that this was a rapid review, instead of scoping or systematic review, we may have missed important published studies. Given that few peer-reviewed studies have specifically targeted family system functioning and child development outcomes, conclusions to date need to be tentative, and future research on these topics is warranted. As the literature develops, more targeted systematic reviews and meta-analyses will be able to provide a more comprehensive overview of the consequences of climate change, and specific climate hazards, for family functioning and specific child development outcomes.

Third, we found very few qualitative studies about the lived experiences of families in the context of climate change. Indeed, reports from agencies like UNICEF and Save The Children do include accounts of family experiences (e.g., UNICEF, 2020), but these sources are not typically peer-reviewed. Future research should use qualitative techniques with wellgrounded methodologies, including interviews, focus groups, ethnographies, and partici­ patory research, to understand families’ experiences when facing acute climate hazards (e.g., extreme weather events) and their needs and perspectives related to chronic climate hazards (e.g., sea-level rise, ecological degradation). Qualitative and quantitative approaches can also help researchers understand how families are already preparing, responding, and adapting in the context of climate change, which can inform future intervention work and policy development.

Finally, current quantitative evidence on the potential consequences of climate change on families is limited by issues of internal and external validity due to methodological approaches that make it difficult to establish causal effects (i.e., confounding) and underrepresentation of specific settings (e.g., low- and- middle-income countries) and groups (e.g., gender diverse

## Conclusion

Climate change poses an unprecedented threat to families worldwide. Acute and chronic climate hazards can disrupt the proximal contexts of development and increase contextual risks, potentially undermining human development across the life course. Without rapid reductions of greenhouse gas emissions at a global level, these impacts will become more severe and widespread. While governments and corporations have the greatest responsibility for mitigating climate change, a bioecological and dynamic systems perspective demonstrates that families can also play a significant role in mitigating climate change and achieving positive outcomes even when facing adversity. There is an urgent need for more research and applied work to understand the links between climate change, families, and human devel­ opment, and also on how to design, implement, and scale evidence-based policies and programs that promote families’ resilience and well-being in the context of climate change.

# Abstract:

We examine empirical and conceptual considerations related to the role of nurturing care for protecting human capital formation in the context of climate change.

Climate change is a pressing global challenge. Heatwaves, wildfires, storms, and floods are becoming more frequent and severe, and their direct impact and aftermath can have long-lasting negative effects on employment, education, healthcare, and access to essen­ tial services. Children are particularly vulnerable to these harms due to their developmen­ tal immaturity and limited capacity to mitigate and avoid risks [1,2]. Consequently, parents and other adult primary caregivers – such as grandparents, relatives, and foster parents (hereafter “caregivers”) – provide the primary buffer between climate hazards and adverse developmental outcomes. They do this through nurturing care, defined as the provision of stable environments that promote children’s health and nutrition, safety and security, opportunities for learning, and emotionally supportive relationships [3]. Despite the central role of nurturing care for children’s life outcomes, it rarely appears in climate change research and policy discourse.

## Nurturing care promotes and protects child development

Children’s need for nurturing care in order to flourish is enshrined in global policy tools like the Nurturing Care Framework [4]. Nurturing care promotes the development of founda­ tional cognitive, social, emotional, language, motor, and executive function skills that predict lifelong learning, health, and adaptive behaviors central to human capital formation [3]. These benefits are well-documented for children living in poverty, forced displacement, conflict zones, and other emergency settings, indicating that nurturing care also promotes the devel­ opment of coping mechanisms to overcome early hardship [3]. Despite this, fewer than one in four young children living in low- and- middle-income countries (LMICs) receive minimally adequate nurturing care, which hampers individual development and societal progress and threatens global policy objectives such as the Sustainable Development Goals - SDGs [5,6]. Climate change will likely exacerbate these challenges further.

There is now extensive evidence that climate change is already harming the healthy devel­ opment of children and adolescents in regions across the world [2,7]. Climate change poses direct and indirect risks to children’s healthy physiological, psychosocial, and neurocognitive development through multiple acute and chronic hazards, such as tropical storms, floods, heatwaves, droughts, altered ecosystems, and sea level rise (Fig 1). When these impacts occur early in life, they can cascade with additive, interactive, and cumulative effects on education, economic participation, and long-term health and wellbeing [1].

## Links between climate change and nurturing care

Evidence from prior crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, shows that contextual stressors can compromise caregivers’ ability to provide nurturing care by undermining health, well­ being, and available material, cognitive, social, and emotional resources. In the context of climate change, extreme weather events can damage and destroy infrastructure, disrupt access to essential services, food and water, and lead to school closures, family separation, and forced displacement – all of which make it more difficult for caregivers to provide for children’s basic needs. Reviews of the evidence indicate robust associations between exposure to disasters and extreme weather events and increased risk of parenting stress and mental health problems such as PTSD, depression, anxiety, substance use, and suicidal behaviors [8]. This mental health burden, in turn, can lead to negative caregiver behaviors, including heightened risk for child physical punishment, reduced learning opportunities, and adverse social and emotional development [8–10].

Caregiving is practically and psychologically demanding. The experience of losing a home or livelihood to flooding, for example, not only undermines material resources but also key cognitive and psychosocial resources critical to providing a nurturing care. It makes it harder for caregivers to regulate their attention and behavioral responses, and raises the risk of inadequate supervision, diminished responsiveness, impaired conflict resolution skills, vio­ lence against children, and intimate partner violence [11]. In this way, climate change erodes caregivers’ capacity to respond and adapt to children’s needs and thus provide them with the nurturing care critical for their development, especially when resources are already stretched.

Climate change impacts on caregivers are inequitably distributed. Within nations, low-­ income families and communities affected by armed conflict, forced displacement, and other adversities are often more vulnerable to exposure to climate related hazards, such as heat stress and flooding, while also having fewer resources to adapt and respond to these stress­ ors. Inequities between rich and poor nations can be even starker: around 89% of the world’s children live in LMICs, which are overwhelmingly located in regions identified as being most vulnerable to climate change [2,12]. As a result, hundreds of millions of caregivers in these regions must contend with already-scarce goods and services in contexts further strained by climate hazards – thus amplifying the risk that caregiving capacity, and therefore child devel­ opment, will be compromised.

The risks for women are especially acute. Across the world, women provide the bulk of nurturing care and are disproportionately vulnerable to climate-related impacts. For instance, due to persistent discriminatory gender-based cultural norms and practices as well as eco­ nomic and political barriers [13], girls and women often have more limited access to financial resources, employment opportunities, and property ownership, making it more difficult to independently respond and adapt to climate-related hazards. In some LMICs, they are also frequently dependent on low or unpaid outdoor labor such as water and fuel collection, which directly exposes them to weather-related hazards such as heat stress. Similarly, in the after­ math of acute weather disasters, displaced women are disproportionately vulnerable to vio­ lence, exploitation, and trafficking, which present immediate risks to the women themselves

## Implications for research and practice

Caregivers provide the first and primary buffer against climate-related hazards, including mitigating and responding to impacts. More must be done to understand their unique vul­ nerabilities. Further conceptual and empirical work are needed to: 1) clarify the domains of nurturing care that are most vulnerable to disruption through exposure to acute and chronic climate-related hazards; 2) identify hazards that pose the most significant simultaneous risks to children’s development and caregivers’ resources through additive, interactive or cumula­ tive effects across the early life course; 3) determine how existing evidence-based programs and policies aimed at promoting nurturing care may need adaptation for climate-affected contexts, and 4) develop gender-sensitive approaches that support caregivers’ mental health and wellbeing so that they can help children to better understand and navigate the psycholog­ ical consequences of living with climate change. Crucially, these efforts must recognize that LMICs are not a monolith. They encompass a vast range of cultural, geographical, and politi­ cal contexts – implying that effective strategies for nurturing care will differ across regions and must be informed by community-level needs, resources, and voices.

Climate change is no longer a future possibility but a current reality affecting caregivers and children across the globe. These impacts undermine children’s health and development directly and indirectly by eroding their core source of protection and support: nurturing care. Fortunately, encouraging examples of effective locally tailored interventions and adaptation are emerging. In Malawi, for instance, village-led early childhood development centers have offered supportive environments for young children in the aftermath of floods and other weather disasters, which help to protect both child development and caregiver wellbeing alike [14]. Likewise, in Bangladesh, community support organizations have paired parental mental health with support with early childhood feeding programs to improve outcomes for caregiv­ ers and children following tropical cyclones [15]. Programs like these that combine practical resources with mental health and educational support demonstrate the potential to maintain and strengthen nurturing care in the face of climate-related impacts.

By investing in and scaling up these and other context-specific strategies – and by elevating women’s voices in decision-making processes – we can ensure that caregivers and children, especially those in under-resourced settings, are better equipped not just to survive but to thrive in a rapidly changing world.
